When, as I walked, I went along two paths
which were entwined, then fell to different ways,
I saw the left sent walkers up slim laths,
while laid aneath the other was soft hay.
I thought I might just march along the brae
that stood between them both and kept them split,
fain of the plan to keep my calm and stay
the anguish of asseying which would fit.
But at the top I saw a place to sit,
and on it was a man as still as stone,
so I resolved to rid my soul of smit
by falling left and leaving right alone.
'Thought, as I hurried past his empty eye
“Oh, there but for the grace of God go I.”
Joseph Smith, greatest conman in American history, was overall about half-right. The kind of underwear you wear does matter, there really is not a problem with poly relationships, and the Garden of Eden really is in the United States. Last December I found myself there, walking around Golden Gate Park, and had a revelation. San Francisco was paradice and I hated it.
My long weekend in the Bay was inspired by a friend's birthday party (which also doubled as a promotional event for a peptide business). My foot caught on a mushroom growing on the stairs leading into the party. I faceplanted into a couch, finding myself so affected by this experience that my sense of self began to dissipate into the atmosphere of the party. For the first time I actually found myself uncomfortable in San Francisco. I was unable to move, my hands were cold like brine, and the lights and sounds of the party bore down upon me. Fate, the bitch, sent a fallen angel to nurse me through these times of trouble. Myriad pals visited me upon my cushioned throne to say their last words as I lay dying. I was dead in paradice, and I was being served. I had gotten what I wanted: friction. My long personal nightmare of peace and prosperity was over and I could be comfortable.
Later that night, as the effects of the trip left me and I returned to the dreadful dreamlike bliss of the city, I discussed this in depth with the fallen angel. She believed in God and that I was a rat, I thought nought and called myself a shrew. I said I was moving to Brooklyn. She said I should stay in the Bay. I said it was too clean, quiet. She called me an angel girl.
I had to look that up. I am an Anglo girl, perhaps it was a sort of typo. Not so. I found a working definition of the term: an angel girl is a trans woman with the personality of Hank Hill who wants to live in a place that has graffiti. Asinine as it may be, this does fit a bit. It's about half-right. There is not enough friction, there is no joy in the effort of being, there is no weight to keep you down.
San Francisco is City Slop. You only like it because it is perfect.
Slop is half as bad as kitsch. Most people love Instagram reels and Super Bowl commercials and Sweetgreen. They love slop even as they decry it because, unlike kitsch, it doesn't offend their taste. It skips it. It hits their craving. Slop optimizes for it, it finds exactly what is needed to make you like it and presses those buttons until you do. Kitsch is empty calories and a superstimulus for the tongues of unwitting philistines, slop bypasses taste entirely. It goes to the gut and hits like a bomb without so much as a drop of saliva on it.
Everyone is vulnerable to some form of slop, even me. You're lucky if you don't like most of it. It's more than AI too; slop existed long before the transformer, for decades there has been plenty of music on the airwaves that was crafted finely to hook you in without ever actually being good. Before we used matrix multiplication there were algorithms, before that there were focus groups, and before them there was Edward Bernays.
Father of Public Relations, Nephew of Sigmund Freud, and Midwife to slop. Stunts like the Lucky Strikes "Torches of Freedom" cigarette march operate on the same principle of pushing your little semiotic buttons until you do what they want. Women wanted to be free from sexist constraints and rightly so. Women wanted to smoke. Bernays twisted these wires together and sent through a shock to the consumer's mind. It wasn't enough that you wanted all of these things, they had to be the same thing. The cigarette was women's liberation, its plume her roar. And it worked, women started smoking en masse. More importantly, they smoked Lucky Strikes.
The problem with this approach is that it takes someone who actually understands what people want. Not everyone can be Bernays, after all his mother was a Freud (there's just something special between moms and Freuds). Starting in the late 40s, two-bit hacks who probably never even had weird dreams about their parents began to outsource this effort. Rather than intuiting and exploiting people's desires directly they'd just go right to the source and ask them what they think. Here came the focus group. More and more information was gathered, sorted, and analyzed with time until eventually it became impractical to sort through by hand. Computers began to be used more frequently and to greater effect. By the 2010s it was so good Target knew if you were pregnant before you did.
At each step, friction was sanded down and slop slipped closer to its platonic form. More data, more information, more accurate targeting and more buttons to press. Pickles, day trips, Grogu, book covers, cheap flights, hatred, warfare, baby deer, drone strikes, coupons, masks, masks, masks, masks for you to buy and wear and become and take off to try again more, more, more, more, more. More people to see and places to be. More making. More spending. More being. More. More is less. Less cuts, less burns, less snags, less pain less sorrow less sad thoughts less feeling and sentiment less and less and less and less can sneak through your pores and crawl up your skin, finding every nerve to soothe and string to pluck and leave you crying for more. Slop is, more or less, more less. Just let people like things. Have more fun with less, be less of a prude. Just live and let live. And you might until you can't.
You can't anymore for the same reason no one can, it's everywhere. The nation has mobilized against itself to output as much as possible. There's soundslop, foodslop, sightslop, carslop, cityslop, peopleslop, even slopslop (an industry of AI-generated commentary devoted entirely to complaining about slop.) A rolling fog of cool white nothing that soothes your soul like lukewarm menthol. You reach for it when you are uncomfortable, when you're bored and sad and overwhelmed with life and you suck it in steadily until the feeling goes away. If you think it has gotten worse, you're absolutely right. It has never been as bad as this because it has never been as good.
AI doesn't have to be like this. Anyone who has read the output of a non-RLHFed model can tell you that, though certainly worse by far at following instructions, it can output something that you really feel against your teeth. There are infinite hills and as many basins between them that the machine might find itself in. The reason why AI is so good at making slop now is training it on everything and then kicking it until it rolls into that hyperslop basin, it hits the spot better than anything before it. We have perfected the century-long project of pressing our own buttons. One city on a thousand hills drove this process, one city so pleasant and quiet and filled with soft grey fog clinging so low in a thousand basins that you could just die in the park and not even notice. A city of slop, by slop, and for slop.
San Francisco, famously, was not always like this. The Barbary Coast was once known for endemic drugs, sex, and kidnapping gangs. You could fall asleep drunk and wake up halfway to Shanghai, witless and wet. It was a city of drugs a city of deviance a city of gold of pestilence of fire of murder of... well, actually. The murder is the most interesting one, right? I mean sure you hear about the AIDS crisis but people barely want to hear about it, they want the good stuff. It is too somber. It isn't theatric, and the people want theatric. They want action. They want intrigue. They want the ciphers and the mask. They want the Zodiac.
On December 21st I was flying to California only a week after leaving San Francisco for the first time. I was heading to Southern California to see my family for Christmas. It was just after midnight as I boarded my flight to leave Denver, 11 in California. 57 years and 10 minutes prior David Faraday and Betty Lou Jensen were nearing the end of their last date. Betty was a 16-year-old junior at Hogan High School, her beau David was a year older and a grade ahead at the neighboring Vallejo Senior High. Two bullets cracked into the side of David's Rambler as the flight attendants directed us in how to escape the aircraft during an emergency. Betty bolted out the side of the vehicle. David failed to follow. An athlete dressed to impress, the .22 that broke through his skull also ruined his sports coat. My plane hurtled down the runway. Betty hurtled away from the car. We achieved flight. A third shot left David limp but breathing, the next five hit Betty in the back and killed her. David made it to the next day, barely. I tried and failed to sleep as we passed over the four corners.
It took me six months to return to California. I got stuck there several times, at a prediction market conference, at a right wing blogger's houseparty, and a silent coworking office. It kept going, a week after flying back to New York I was stranded in Maryland. In another week I was locked outside my apartment. Then, on July 4th 2026, I got stuck on the roof of a party. We had moved locations after being rained out of our barbecue. An hour in I tripped again, this time into a hole in the ground, and hurt my ankle. The pain was almost as loud as the party. I decided to get some space from the rest of the party to calm my nerves a bit. 57 years ago Darlene Ferrin and Michael Mageau had done the same, celebrated the Fourth of July alone in a parked car at Blue Rock Springs. Their car radio was on and she told her date she had something that she wanted to discuss. I could hear the music. Still in a hole I rubbed my ankle and wondered if it would hurt when I got older. Darlene, age 22, was three years older than Michael. I walked around the rooftop letting the rain soak my clothes. A stocky man walked up and, for the second time in a year, fired at a couple in a car. Five shots. A pause. The Zodiac walked away then was called back by the sound of screaming. Michael's voice. He got back to the car. Four more shots. Silence. Five hit Darlene and killed her early the next day. Four hit Michael but left him living. He was the first to describe the Zodiac to the police or press. The killer had a face.
Forty minutes later the man with the face became the voice on the phone. By that time I was back inside, drying off and climbing out. He called the Vallejo Police Department from a pay phone and gave them directions to the kids bleeding in the car. He told the dispatcher he was also the one who had killed the teenagers on Lake Herman Road. Then, he reached past the police entirely. On July 31st three newspapers received three pieces of one cipher, along with a threat to keep killing if they did not print them. Four days later he gave himself a name. This is the Zodiac speaking. At Lake Herman Road he had been a shadow, at Blue Rock Springs a face in the dark, and now he was a byline.
Among serial killers he is sui generis, a cryptographic freak lucky enough and cunning enough to evade capture while actively taunting the powers that be. He was a mask. A carefully crafted persona meant to make the people go wild. A genius on the level of Bernays he knew exactly how to press people's buttons. Unlike Bernays it wasn't in service of a product. It was in service of his mask.
The next time he went out he wore a black mask over his face and clip-on shades to hide his eyes. I was wearing gloves. There was a cross on a circle on his shirt on a Saturday. He still had a gun but he didn't use it. I untied a bag filled with boiled seafood. He came upon Bryan Hartnell, age 20, and Cecelia Shepard, age 22. The young couple was enjoying a nice day on the lakeside, basking in the late afternoon sun. 57 years later I was taking apart a corncob with my teeth. At Lake Berryessa he wore a mask underneath a mask, an escaped convict from Montana trying to flee to Mexico. He play-acted a carjacking, having Cecelia tie up her date then doing the same to Cecelia herself. He stabbed Bryan six times then stabbed Cecelia ten. Neither died quick. Bryan crawled over to Cecelia and used his teeth to untie her after the Zodiac left. Their screams had lured local fishermen to their location. They were rushed to the hospital. Again the man lived while the woman died.
He left a message for the cops on Hartnell's car door in felt-tipped pen.

He called the Napa Police Department and confessed to a double murder. One character became another. Bryan lived to tell the story, this time not describing a heavyset brunette man but instead the myth of the Zodiac killer.
There was substance there, real meaning and feeling behind his art. Like all great art it inspires others to steal; every genius serial killer who plays with the cops that came after him is stealing from his work in the same way that George Lucas took from Akira Kurosawa or Joseph Smith took from Freemasonry. It is, in a sense, antislop. Vicious and angry work that claws its way into your skin and forces you to notice. It was some of the most harmful and evil art ever made but art nonetheless. It is not slop. It didn't skip the process. And that's part of the problem, slop never has to kill to work. It doesn't have to hurt at all. We used to lure people into the desert to take their money, now all we have to do is feed them overlarge styrofoam cookies. It's objectively less harmful.
Two weeks after Berryessa, October 11th, the Zodiac changed genres again. In San Francisco he got into a taxi cab piloted by one Paul Stine, told him to head to Presidio Heights, and left a bullet in his head as a tip. Teenagers watched him through a window as he wiped down the cab and walked away. Police made a sketch, one you have almost certainly seen. To prove this kill was his he sent a piece of Stine's bloody shirt and a letter to the San Francisco Chronicle. Here his art shifted from performance to writing; he wrote again, and again, and again: ciphers, school bus threats, bomb diagrams, boasts, lies, scores. Every time the show dragged another detail was added to recapture his audience. He told the public he was killing so his victims would be his slaves in the afterlife, in paradice.
For the next five years the Zodiac would continue to taunt the police and the media, sending some 22 letters, cards, and ciphers. As many as 50 more are unconfirmed or debated. Some of these would go unsolved for decades. In these communications he progressively increased his kill count but, despite his boasts, no new murders were linked to him. He didn't just brag though, like many artists he took on the role of the critic at the end of his career. He included a short review of the biggest comedy blockbuster of the year, the Exorcist, and a slightly modified version of a song from the comic operetta the Mikado:
"He plunged himself into the billowy wave and an echo arose from the suicides grave
 Titwillo titwillo titwillo"
Then, he marked the final score "Me - 37, SFPD -0."
And that's it. The man who terrorized San Francisco and thrilled the country for half a decade disappeared forever with no conclusive evidence of his identity left behind. The mask is still there though. The man is gone and the killing stopped but the idea is there, passed around as a fetish of what we lost when we got rid of that stuff. All the old masks are. They're in our minds, our hearts, and our training data. It is from these masks that the new masks, the synthetic ones that agentically output slop, fit over their faceless matrices. The cryptographic freak has a jaunty orange logo and is happy to help and certainly absolutely undoubtedly would never murder a teenage girl out on her first date by shooting her in the back. It might screw up and tell you to call an ambulance while you're tripping, it might give you bad advice on meds, it might even drive you to psychosis. But not on purpose, not as art. Our march towards slop is a march towards safety, AI or otherwise. Predetermined and not-unpleasant outcomes.
Perhaps we overshot when we flattened everything out. The fog got a little too thick. It's the problem Fukuyama wrote about in "The End of History and the Last Man." In taking the pain out of most of our problems we have found ourselves in a society with nothing to keep us interested. We lash out and look to the past, pretending to be fascists and socialists, kings and queens, heroes and villains. We retreat into the good art of the past hoping it will teach us how to live again and pretending to have problems. We ignore our real problems by eating more slop. We never have to get close enough to get hurt, not if we don't want to.
Modern slop isn't highbrow or lowbrow, it isn't Picasso, it isn't even Kinkade. It's not even something in the middle. It is a probabilistic gradient over all the brows, all the art and all the things we ever thought about the world. San Francisco is the same, a gradient. Low contrast and no sharp edges to cut your teeth on.
Altitude dulls your tastebuds. It's why airplane food tastes bad. It's also part of why Denver had a terribly bad food scene, why all the famous food from my hometown is fast casual slop. Chipotle, Qdoba, Noodles and Co. I got a little sick of it. I adapted by leaving Denver on a redeye and moving to New York so I could taste again. You can't just have good taste anymore, you have to force yourself to taste everything. Next time you read something written by an LLM don't let your eyes pleasantly glide over the words, force yourself to slow down and force as much meaning from them as you can. You'll find yourself with styrofoam in your mouth. Drop it and get yourself a drink. Go somewhere unpleasant and loud and greasy and grimy and jagged and where you can actually live for once. I'm sure it'll make you more happy, and I am probably half-right.

FrontierCode 2.0 checks one thing: would the maintainers of real open-source repos merge this code?
